title: Annual Research Review: Infant Development, Autism, and ADHD—Early Pathways to Emerging Disorders

subsections.section_title: Neurodevelopmental Trajectories in Infancy: Foundations of Autism and ADHD
subsections.subsection_title: Early motor and sensory processing differences
subsections.content:
Emerging evidence indicates that infants who later receive diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibit subtle but detectable differences in motor development and sensory processing as early as 3–6 months of age. Infants at elevated risk for ASD show reduced spontaneous movement variability, delayed acquisition of gross motor milestones such as sitting and reaching, and atypical limb coordination patterns, which may reflect underlying cerebellar and corticospinal circuit disruptions [1]. Similarly, infants who later develop ADHD demonstrate increased motor activity and reduced motor inhibition in structured tasks, even before the onset of attentional symptoms [2].

Sensory processing differences are also evident in the first year, with infants at risk for ASD exhibiting heightened or diminished responses to auditory, tactile, and visual stimuli. For instance, reduced habituation to repeated auditory tones and atypical visual tracking of moving objects have been documented in high-risk infants as early as 6 months [3]. These patterns are associated with altered neural responses in primary sensory cortices and the superior temporal sulcus [4]. In contrast, infants who develop ADHD show less consistent sensory modulation, with increased distractibility to irrelevant stimuli and reduced sensory filtering [5].

Longitudinal studies suggest that these motor and sensory differences often precede and predict later social-communicative deficits, supporting their role as early biomarkers [6]. Multimodal analyses reveal that motor delays and sensory atypicalities co-occur more frequently in infants who develop comorbid ASD and ADHD than in those with either diagnosis alone [7]. Together, these findings underscore the importance of early motor and sensory assessment in identifying neurodevelopmental risk trajectories.

subsections.section_title: Neurodevelopmental Trajectories in Infancy: Foundations of Autism and ADHD
subsections.subsection_title: Social attention and joint engagement in infancy
subsections.content:
Infants at elevated risk for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) demonstrate early deviations in social attention and joint engagement, often preceding overt behavioral symptoms. Longitudinal studies reveal reduced orienting to social stimuli, including diminished eye contact and slower responses to name calling, as early as 6–12 months of age in high-risk infants who later receive an ASD diagnosis [1]. These deficits are not merely quantitative but qualitative, manifesting as atypical patterns of gaze following and reduced initiation of joint attention behaviors such as pointing or showing objects to caregivers [2]. In contrast, infants who develop typical social skills show increasing consistency in shared attention episodes, whereas those who later develop ASD exhibit declining or unstable engagement over time [3].

Similar patterns are observed in infants at familial risk for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), though the profile differs: while joint attention initiation may be relatively preserved, sustained attention during social interactions is often disrupted by distractibility and reduced persistence [4]. Neuroimaging studies corroborate these behavioral findings, showing altered activation in the posterior superior temporal sulcus and medial prefrontal cortex during social attention tasks in high-risk infants [5]. Importantly, the co-occurrence of social attention deficits and regulatory difficulties in infancy predicts later dual diagnosis of ASD and ADHD more robustly than either domain alone [6]. These early markers suggest that disruptions in the foundational architecture of social engagement may represent a transdiagnostic vulnerability pathway.

subsections.section_title: Neurodevelopmental Trajectories in Infancy: Foundations of Autism and ADHD
subsections.subsection_title: Regulatory and arousal patterns
subsections.content:
Infants who later receive diagnoses of ASD or ADHD often exhibit atypical regulatory and arousal patterns in the first year of life, including heightened reactivity to sensory stimuli, prolonged distress responses, and difficulties in state regulation. Longitudinal studies have shown that infants at familial risk for ASD display elevated baseline cortisol levels and reduced habituation to repeated auditory stimuli, suggesting dysregulated stress response systems ref [14]. Similarly, infants who later develop ADHD show increased motor activity and reduced ability to self-soothe during caregiving interactions, which may reflect underlying deficits in top-down arousal modulation ref [15]. These regulatory differences often precede overt social or attentional symptoms and are predictive of later diagnostic outcomes when combined with other early markers.

Emerging evidence indicates that atypical arousal patterns in infancy are not isolated but interact with sensory and social processing deficits. For instance, infants with co-occurring regulatory and social attention impairments demonstrate a significantly higher likelihood of dual ASD-ADHD diagnosis by age 3, suggesting a shared neurodevelopmental pathway ref [4]. Furthermore, longitudinal analyses reveal that infants with poor state regulation at 6 months are more likely to exhibit emotional dysregulation and sleep disturbances at 18 months, which in turn correlate with later behavioral challenges ref [16]. These findings underscore the importance of monitoring regulatory behaviors as early indicators of neurodevelopmental risk.

subsections.section_title: Genetic, Epigenetic, and Prenatal Influences on Risk Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Heritability and polygenic risk scores in infancy
subsections.content:
Genetic influences on autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are well-established, with heritability estimates ranging from 70% to 90% for both conditions. In infancy, polygenic risk scores (PRS) derived from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have begun to predict early behavioral and neurodevelopmental trajectories, even before clinical symptoms emerge. Infants with higher ASD-PRS show reduced social orienting and atypical visual attention patterns, independent of familial diagnosis, suggesting that genetic liability manifests in early neurobehavioral phenotypes [1]. Similarly, ADHD-PRS in infancy correlates with elevated motor activity and diminished attentional persistence, indicating a biological substrate for early hyperactivity and inattention [2]. These associations persist after controlling for parental psychopathology, supporting the direct influence of common genetic variants on infant development [3].

Recent studies have demonstrated that PRS can stratify risk within high-risk infant sibling cohorts, identifying subgroups with accelerated developmental deviations despite similar familial loading [4]. For instance, infants with high ASD-PRS and no diagnosed older sibling still exhibit reduced eye contact and delayed social smiling, mirroring patterns seen in diagnosed probands [5]. Moreover, cross-disorder PRS analyses reveal shared genetic architecture between ASD and ADHD in infancy, with overlapping polygenic signals predicting co-occurring regulatory and attentional difficulties [6]. These findings underscore that genetic risk operates continuously across the population, with early behavioral markers serving as proximal indicators of underlying neurodevelopmental vulnerability [7].

subsections.section_title: Genetic, Epigenetic, and Prenatal Influences on Risk Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Prenatal exposures and fetal programming
subsections.content:
Prenatal environmental exposures, including maternal stress, infection, nutritional deficiencies, and toxin exposure, have been implicated in altering fetal neurodevelopment and increasing risk for ASD and ADHD. Maternal immune activation due to infection during pregnancy is associated with altered microglial function and cytokine profiles in the fetal brain, which may disrupt synaptic pruning and cortical circuit formation [1]. Similarly, elevated maternal cortisol levels, resulting from chronic stress, can cross the placental barrier and affect fetal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis development, contributing to later emotional dysregulation and attentional deficits [2].

Nutritional factors such as folate, choline, and omega-3 fatty acid availability during gestation modulate neurodevelopmental trajectories; inadequate folate intake has been linked to increased ASD risk, while optimal levels appear protective, potentially through epigenetic regulation of neural gene expression [3]. Exposure to environmental toxins like air pollution (PM2.5), phthalates, and heavy metals has also been associated with altered neurodevelopment, with epidemiological studies showing dose-dependent increases in ADHD-like behaviors and social communication impairments in exposed offspring [4].

These exposures may act synergistically with genetic vulnerability, where fetal programming mechanisms—such as altered DNA methylation and histone modification—mediate long-term changes in gene expression without altering the DNA sequence [5]. Animal models demonstrate that prenatal stress combined with genetic risk variants amplifies behavioral phenotypes relevant to ASD and ADHD, supporting a gene-environment interaction model [6]. Longitudinal human cohorts confirm that prenatal adversity interacts with polygenic risk to predict earlier onset and greater severity of neurodevelopmental symptoms [7].

subsections.section_title: Genetic, Epigenetic, and Prenatal Influences on Risk Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Epigenetic modifications and gene-environment interactions
subsections.content:
Epigenetic modifications serve as a critical interface between genetic susceptibility and prenatal environmental exposures in the development of ASD and ADHD. DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA regulation have been implicated in mediating the effects of maternal stress, nutrition, and toxin exposure on fetal neurodevelopment. For instance, prenatal stress has been associated with altered methylation patterns in genes regulating the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, such as NR3C1 and FKBP5, which correlate with later emotional dysregulation and attentional deficits in offspring. Similarly, maternal folate and choline levels influence methylation of neurodevelopmental genes, with both deficiency and excess linked to atypical synaptic pruning and cortical connectivity.

Emerging evidence demonstrates that epigenetic marks can amplify or buffer polygenic risk, creating differential phenotypic outcomes even among genetically similar infants. Studies in infant cohorts have shown that high polygenic risk for ASD combined with prenatal air pollution exposure is associated with distinct methylation signatures in immune and neuronal pathways not observed in low-risk infants. These gene-environment epigenetic interactions may underlie the heterogeneity in early behavioral phenotypes, including sensory hypersensitivity and social attention deficits. Longitudinal analyses further suggest that epigenetic changes in cord blood and infant buccal cells can predict later diagnostic outcomes, highlighting their potential as early biomarkers.

Importantly, epigenetic modifications are dynamic and potentially reversible, offering mechanistic insight into intervention targets. Animal models and human cohort studies confirm that nutritional supplementation or stress reduction during pregnancy can normalize methylation profiles and mitigate behavioral risk, underscoring the modifiable nature of these pathways.

subsections.section_title: Behavioral and Cognitive Markers: From Infancy to Toddlerhood
subsections.subsection_title: Language acquisition delays and pragmatic deficits
subsections.content:
Language acquisition delays and pragmatic deficits are among the earliest and most robust behavioral markers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) emerging between 12 and 36 months. Infants later diagnosed with ASD often exhibit reduced vocalizations, delayed first words, and atypical prosody, even when nonverbal cognitive skills are preserved. Longitudinal studies show that reduced babbling complexity and diminished response to name by 12 months predict later language impairment and ASD diagnosis, independent of general developmental delay ref [22]. Pragmatic deficits—such as failure to initiate joint attention, lack of communicative gestures, and impaired turn-taking—are distinguishable from mere expressive delays and are more specific to ASD than to other neurodevelopmental conditions ref [12]. These deficits often precede syntactic or semantic delays, suggesting a core disruption in social motivation or intentionality underlying language development.

In contrast, children with ADHD typically show less pronounced early language delays, though they may exhibit disorganized speech, tangentiality, and reduced conversational reciprocity by toddlerhood, reflecting underlying attentional and inhibitory control challenges ref [8]. However, co-occurring ASD and ADHD symptoms are associated with more severe pragmatic impairments than either condition alone, indicating additive or synergistic effects on social communication ref [12]. Recent evidence from high-risk infant sibling cohorts confirms that pragmatic language deficits, measured via caregiver report and observational coding, are more predictive of ASD than motor or sensory atypicalities alone ref [24]. Early identification of these profiles enables targeted intervention during critical windows of neural plasticity.

subsections.section_title: Behavioral and Cognitive Markers: From Infancy to Toddlerhood
subsections.subsection_title: Executive function and attentional control in toddlers
subsections.content:
Executive function (EF) and attentional control begin to emerge as discernible constructs in toddlers between 18 and 36 months, with atypical trajectories often preceding clinical diagnoses of ASD and ADHD. Toddlers at familial risk for ASD show reduced ability to shift attention flexibly and sustain focus during structured tasks, even in the absence of language delays, suggesting a core deficit in cognitive control rather than secondary to social communication impairments ref [33]. Similarly, toddlers with elevated ADHD polygenic risk exhibit diminished inhibitory control and increased impulsivity in delay-of-gratification paradigms, independent of hyperactivity levels ref [34]. Longitudinal studies indicate that poor performance on tasks requiring working memory and response inhibition at 24 months predicts later ADHD symptoms at age 5, with effect sizes comparable to those of parent-reported behavioral ratings ref [35]. In ASD, restricted interests may co-occur with inflexible attentional set-shifting, manifesting as perseverative behavior in object-sorting tasks, which distinguishes them from general developmental delay ref [36]. These EF deficits are often detectable before language or social deficits become pronounced, highlighting their potential as early biomarkers.

Neural correlates of these behavioral profiles include reduced activation in the prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate during attentional control tasks, as measured by fNIRS and EEG, particularly in infants later diagnosed with ASD or ADHD ref [37]. Moreover, co-occurring sensory modulation difficulties exacerbate attentional lapses, suggesting that EF impairments in early development are not isolated but embedded within broader regulatory dysfunctions ref [38]. The specificity of these markers is further supported by studies showing that toddlers with ASD or ADHD exhibit distinct patterns of EF disruption compared to those with global developmental delay or language-only impairments ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Behavioral and Cognitive Markers: From Infancy to Toddlerhood
subsections.subsection_title: Repetitive behaviors and restricted interests in infancy
subsections.content:
Repetitive behaviors and restricted interests (RBRI) emerge as early as 12 months in infants at familial risk for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), often preceding formal diagnosis. These include repetitive motor movements such as hand flapping, object spinning, and unusual sensory exploration, which are more frequent and persistent than in typically developing peers. Longitudinal studies indicate that the emergence and escalation of such behaviors between 12 and 24 months are predictive of later ASD diagnosis, particularly when co-occurring with social communication delays ref [39]. Unlike transient motor stereotypies seen in some typically developing infants, RBRI in ASD-risk infants show greater rigidity, resistance to redirection, and association with sensory sensitivities ref [40].

Emerging evidence suggests that RBRI in infancy may reflect underlying neural atypicalities in sensorimotor integration and corticostriatal circuitry, with fMRI and EEG studies revealing altered connectivity in regions supporting habit formation and reward processing ref [41]. These behaviors are less consistently observed in infants at risk for ADHD alone, distinguishing them as a more specific marker for ASD trajectories ref [42]. However, in co-occurring ASD/ADHD profiles, RBRI may be compounded by hyperactivity, complicating phenotypic delineation ref [43].

The specificity of RBRI for ASD is further supported by comparative studies showing that infants with non-ASD developmental delays exhibit fewer and less structured repetitive behaviors ref [44]. Early identification of RBRI, particularly when quantified via standardized observational tools like the Autism Observation Scale for Infants, enhances predictive accuracy when integrated with social attention and regulatory markers ref [45].

subsections.section_title: Parent-Infant Interactions and Environmental Moderators
subsections.subsection_title: Synchrony and contingent responsiveness in caregiving
subsections.content:
Synchrony and contingent responsiveness in caregiving are critical behavioral mechanisms that shape early social-emotional development and may buffer or exacerbate risk for neurodevelopmental disorders such as ASD and ADHD. Infants who experience high levels of contingent maternal responsiveness—where caregivers accurately perceive and timely respond to infant cues—demonstrate enhanced regulatory capacity and more robust social engagement, even in the presence of genetic vulnerability ref [46]. Longitudinal studies show that disruptions in dyadic synchrony, such as delayed or mismatched responses to infant bids for attention, are associated with reduced joint attention and increased social withdrawal in infants at familial risk for ASD ref [47]. These patterns are detectable as early as 6 months and predict later social communication deficits independent of genetic risk profiles ref [48].

Contingent responsiveness also modulates neural development; infants with high-quality caregiver interactions exhibit more mature prefrontal and limbic system activation during social tasks, suggesting a neurobiological pathway through which caregiving quality influences developmental trajectories ref [49]. In contrast, low contingency is linked to atypical EEG patterns in social processing regions, particularly in infants with elevated polygenic risk for ASD ref [50]. Interventions that enhance parental sensitivity, such as video-feedback programs, have been shown to improve synchrony and reduce the emergence of early ASD-like behaviors in high-risk dyads ref [51]. These findings underscore that caregiver responsiveness is not merely a correlate but an active moderator of early risk expression, offering a promising target for preventive strategies.

subsections.section_title: Parent-Infant Interactions and Environmental Moderators
subsections.subsection_title: Socioeconomic and cultural influences on early detection
subsections.content:
Socioeconomic status (SES) significantly influences the timing and accuracy of early detection for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in infancy. Lower SES is associated with delayed diagnostic evaluations, reduced access to developmental screening tools, and fewer opportunities for early intervention, even when risk signs are present ref [54]. Disparities in healthcare access, transportation, and provider availability contribute to these delays, particularly in underserved communities ref [55]. Cultural beliefs about child development and stigma surrounding neurodevelopmental diagnoses can further hinder recognition of early risk signs, with some families interpreting atypical behaviors as temperamentally normal or spiritually significant rather than clinically relevant ref [56].

Language barriers and mistrust of medical systems in immigrant and minority populations also impede early detection, as standardized screening instruments are often not culturally or linguistically adapted ref [57]. Studies show that caregivers from low-SES backgrounds are less likely to receive timely feedback from pediatricians about developmental concerns, even when screening tools indicate risk ref [58]. Moreover, cultural norms around eye contact, responsiveness, and emotional expression may lead clinicians to misinterpret normative variations as pathological, resulting in both under- and over-diagnosis across populations ref [59].

Efforts to improve equity in early detection must include culturally competent screening protocols, community-based outreach, and training for providers in implicit bias ref [60]. Integrating home-based assessments and partnering with community health workers have shown promise in bridging detection gaps in marginalized populations ref [61]. Without addressing these systemic and cultural moderators, early intervention programs risk exacerbating existing disparities in neurodevelopmental outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Parent-Infant Interactions and Environmental Moderators
subsections.subsection_title: Family stress and parental mental health
subsections.content:
Elevated family stress and parental mental health challenges, particularly maternal depression and anxiety, are consistently associated with attenuated caregiver responsiveness and altered infant behavioral trajectories in those at familial risk for ASD or ADHD. Chronic stress can disrupt the neurobiological regulation of caregiving behaviors, impairing the quality of contingent interactions that typically buffer early risk signs [1]. Longitudinal studies indicate that parents experiencing depressive symptoms exhibit reduced sensitivity to infant cues, which may exacerbate emerging social attention deficits and regulatory difficulties in high-risk infants [2]. These effects are not merely correlational; experimental evidence suggests that interventions targeting parental mental health can improve infant social engagement and reduce the expression of early risk behaviors [3].

Paternal mental health also plays a critical, though less studied, role. Fathers with elevated anxiety or depression show diminished engagement in play and communication, which may independently contribute to delays in infant language and social development [4]. Moreover, the co-occurrence of parental psychopathology and socioeconomic hardship amplifies developmental risk, creating a compounding effect on infant neurobehavioral outcomes [5]. Biological mechanisms, including altered cortisol rhythms and epigenetic modifications in stress-responsive genes, have been documented in infants of parents with chronic mental health conditions, suggesting a pathway through which parental distress may biologically embed risk [6].

Culturally informed models of care emphasize the need to distinguish normative stress responses from clinically significant pathology, particularly in marginalized communities where stigma may deter help-seeking [7]. Screening for parental mental health within early developmental surveillance programs is associated with improved detection of at-risk infants and more timely access to family-centered interventions [8]. Integrating mental health support into early intervention frameworks is thus not merely adjunctive but foundational to mitigating the expression of neurodevelopmental risk.

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging and Biomarker Research in Early Development
subsections.subsection_title: Structural and functional brain connectivity in infancy
subsections.content:
Emerging neuroimaging studies using infant-friendly MRI and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) have revealed atypical structural connectivity in infants at familial risk for ASD and ADHD, particularly in white matter tracts supporting social and attentional networks. Reduced fractional anisotropy in the arcuate fasciculus and superior longitudinal fasciculus has been associated with later language and attentional deficits, suggesting early disruption in long-range cortical connectivity ref [64]. Functional connectivity analyses via resting-state fMRI and fNIRS demonstrate altered synchrony within the default mode and salience networks as early as 6 months of age in high-risk infants, with hypoconnectivity between frontal and temporal regions predicting later social communication impairments ref [65].

Longitudinal studies have further shown that aberrant functional connectivity patterns in infancy, particularly in the fronto-parietal and cingulo-opercular networks, precede behavioral symptoms and correlate with polygenic risk scores for ASD and ADHD ref [66]. Infants who later receive a diagnosis exhibit hyperconnectivity within local sensory networks alongside reduced global integration, a pattern consistent with the 'underconnectivity' theory of autism but also observed in early ADHD trajectories ref [67]. These findings are corroborated by multimodal studies combining DTI with EEG, revealing that structural delays in myelination coincide with atypical gamma-band synchrony during social stimulus processing ref [68].

Importantly, connectivity profiles in infancy show differential trajectories between ASD and ADHD risk groups, with ASD-associated patterns characterized by more pronounced local overconnectivity and ASD+ADHD comorbidity risk linked to widespread hypoconnectivity across attentional systems ref [69]. Recent advances in machine learning applied to infant connectomes have enabled predictive models of later diagnosis with moderate accuracy, highlighting the potential of connectivity biomarkers for early stratification ref [70].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging and Biomarker Research in Early Development
subsections.subsection_title: Eye-tracking and pupillometry as behavioral biomarkers
subsections.content:
Eye-tracking and pupillometry have emerged as sensitive, non-invasive tools for detecting early behavioral biomarkers of ASD and ADHD in infancy, prior to the emergence of overt diagnostic symptoms. Infants who later receive an ASD diagnosis exhibit reduced attention to social stimuli, including diminished gaze toward eyes and faces, even as early as 6 months of age, suggesting atypical social orienting as a core early marker ref [60]. Similarly, reduced joint attention and prolonged latency in orienting to social cues have been prospectively linked to later ASD diagnosis in high-risk siblings ref [13]. Pupillometry, which measures autonomic arousal via pupil dilation, reveals atypical reactivity to social and sensory stimuli in infants at familial risk for neurodevelopmental disorders, with hyper-reactivity to non-social stimuli and blunted responses to social cues observed in those who later develop ASD ref [51].

In ADHD, infant pupillary responses during attentional tasks show heightened baseline arousal and impaired modulation under cognitive load, reflecting early dysregulation of noradrenergic systems ref [42]. Eye-tracking studies further demonstrate reduced sustained attention to dynamic social scenes and increased distractibility in infants with elevated ADHD polygenic risk, even in the absence of motor hyperactivity ref [15]. These measures are particularly valuable because they are objective, quantifiable, and compatible with infant-friendly protocols, enabling longitudinal assessment in naturalistic settings. Multimodal integration of eye-tracking with EEG and fNIRS further enhances predictive power by linking behavioral attention patterns to underlying neural dynamics ref [59].

subsections.section_title: Neuroimaging and Biomarker Research in Early Development
subsections.subsection_title: Multimodal biomarker integration
subsections.content:
Integrating multimodal biomarkers in infancy offers a powerful approach to identifying early neural signatures of ASD and ADHD before behavioral symptoms emerge. Combining structural and functional neuroimaging with physiological and behavioral measures enhances predictive accuracy by capturing complementary aspects of neurodevelopment. For instance, concurrent fNIRS and eye-tracking have revealed that atypical prefrontal activation during social attention tasks co-occurs with reduced gaze persistence, providing a more robust risk profile than either modality alone. Similarly, EEG-derived oscillatory patterns coupled with pupillometric indices of arousal regulation have been shown to predict later diagnostic outcomes with higher sensitivity than single-modality models. Recent studies have demonstrated that integrating polygenic risk scores with infant brain connectivity patterns improves classification of infants who will later receive ASD or ADHD diagnoses, reflecting the interplay between genetic liability and early neural dynamics. Multimodal machine learning frameworks that fuse DTI, EEG, and behavioral metrics have successfully distinguished infants with dual risk for ASD and ADHD from those with single-diagnosis risk or typical development. Such integrative models are particularly valuable in heterogeneous populations, where single biomarkers often lack specificity.

Furthermore, combining cortisol stress reactivity measures with sensory processing EEG signatures has identified subgroups of infants with co-occurring regulatory and sensory atypicalities, which are strongly predictive of later dual diagnosis. These approaches move beyond symptom-based classification toward biologically grounded phenotypes, enabling earlier and more targeted interventions.

subsections.section_title: Early Intervention Strategies and Translational Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Parent-mediated interventions (e.g., JASPER, COPE)
subsections.content:
Parent-mediated interventions have emerged as a cornerstone of early intervention for infants showing early signs of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), leveraging the caregiver’s central role in shaping developmental trajectories. Programs such as JASPER (Joint Attention, Symbolic Play, Engagement, and Regulation) and COPE (Creating Opportunities for Parent Empowerment) are grounded in behavioral and developmental frameworks, aiming to enhance parental responsiveness, joint attention, and emotional regulation through structured coaching. Randomized controlled trials demonstrate that JASPER significantly improves infant social communication and reduces ASD symptom severity when delivered during the second year of life, with gains maintained at 12-month follow-up ref [51]. Similarly, COPE has shown efficacy in reducing regulatory difficulties and improving parent-infant synchrony in high-risk infants, particularly when tailored to address co-occurring sensory and attentional challenges ref [46]. These interventions operate through mechanisms of increased contingent responsiveness, which in turn supports neural development of social attention networks ref [49].

Emerging evidence suggests that the timing and fidelity of implementation critically influence outcomes, with earlier initiation (before 18 months) correlating with greater gains in language and social engagement ref [48]. Moreover, adaptations of these models for diverse cultural and socioeconomic contexts have improved accessibility without compromising efficacy, highlighting the importance of culturally responsive delivery ref [60]. While most research has focused on ASD, preliminary applications in ADHD-risk infants indicate that parent-mediated strategies targeting attentional regulation and emotional co-regulation can mitigate emerging hyperactivity and impulsivity ref [53]. Long-term follow-ups reveal sustained improvements in adaptive functioning, though effects on core ADHD symptoms require further longitudinal study ref [16]. The integration of real-time behavioral feedback and digital tools is expanding scalability, positioning parent-mediated approaches as viable, scalable components of early intervention systems.

subsections.section_title: Early Intervention Strategies and Translational Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Neuroplasticity-based approaches in infancy
subsections.content:
Neuroplasticity-based approaches in infancy leverage the heightened malleability of the developing brain to modify atypical trajectories associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). These interventions target core neural circuits involved in social attention, sensory processing, and executive function, often using enriched environmental stimuli or structured sensory-motor experiences to promote adaptive reorganization. For instance, infant-directed visual and auditory stimulation protocols have been shown to enhance cortical responsiveness in high-risk infants, with EEG markers indicating improved neural synchrony in the temporal and prefrontal regions ref [15]. Similarly, sensorimotor enrichment programs have demonstrated effects on white matter integrity, particularly in the superior longitudinal fasciculus, correlating with later improvements in attentional control ref [67].

Emerging evidence suggests that neuroplasticity can be harnessed through non-invasive, developmentally appropriate paradigms such as rhythmic auditory-motor entrainment, which modulates cerebello-thalamo-cortical connectivity and reduces motor stereotypies in infants with familial risk for ASD ref [57]. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) studies further reveal that targeted social engagement tasks can normalize prefrontal activation patterns in infants who later develop ADHD-like symptoms ref [32]. These findings underscore the potential of early, brain-guided interventions to alter developmental trajectories before behavioral symptoms fully crystallize.

subsections.section_title: Early Intervention Strategies and Translational Pathways
subsections.subsection_title: Challenges in early diagnosis and implementation
subsections.content:
Early diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in infancy remains challenging due to the subtle, overlapping nature of behavioral precursors and the lack of definitive biomarkers. While tools like the Autism Observation Scale for Infants show predictive utility, their sensitivity varies across cultural and socioeconomic contexts, leading to disparities in identification rates ref [68]. Socioeconomic status significantly influences access to screening and diagnostic services, with underserved populations experiencing delayed or missed diagnoses ref [66]. Language barriers and cultural interpretations of infant behavior further complicate early detection, as caregivers and clinicians may misattribute atypical behaviors to normative variation or parenting styles ref [56]. Moreover, the heterogeneity of early phenotypes—such as motor, sensory, and attentional differences—often results in diagnostic uncertainty, particularly in infants with dual risk for ASD and ADHD ref [44]. Even when risk is identified, implementation of early intervention is hindered by fragmented healthcare systems, provider shortages, and inconsistent referral pathways ref [40].

Cultural perceptions of child development also shape help-seeking behaviors, with some communities underutilizing developmental screening due to stigma or mistrust in medical systems ref [16]. Community health worker models have shown promise in bridging these gaps, yet scalability remains limited ref [46]. Finally, the absence of standardized, culturally adapted screening protocols across diverse populations undermines the generalizability of early detection efforts, highlighting the need for equity-centered diagnostic frameworks.

subsections.section_title: Convergent and Divergent Pathways: Overlap and Distinction Between ASD and ADHD in Early Development
subsections.subsection_title: Shared risk factors: attentional dysregulation and sensory sensitivity
subsections.content:
Attentional dysregulation and sensory sensitivity represent two core shared risk factors in the early developmental pathways of both autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Infants at elevated risk for either condition frequently exhibit difficulties in attentional persistence, heightened reactivity to sensory stimuli, and impaired modulation of arousal states, which may precede overt diagnostic symptoms. Longitudinal studies indicate that atypical sensory processing, particularly in auditory and visual modalities, is evident in infancy and predicts later emergence of both ASD and ADHD traits, suggesting a common neurobehavioral substrate [16]. Similarly, dysregulated attentional control, measured through tasks of orienting and disengagement, is associated with polygenic risk for both disorders and correlates with later executive function deficits [13].

Neurophysiological evidence further supports convergence: infants with familial risk for ASD or ADHD show overlapping patterns of altered prefrontal activation during attentional tasks, as well as atypical EEG signatures of sensory gating and habituation [11]. These shared neural correlates may reflect underlying disruptions in fronto-parietal and salience networks that regulate attentional focus and sensory filtering. Moreover, sensory over-responsivity and attentional lability often co-occur in high-risk infants, with multimodal analyses revealing that co-occurring motor and sensory atypicalities significantly increase the likelihood of dual diagnostic outcomes [17].

subsections.section_title: Convergent and Divergent Pathways: Overlap and Distinction Between ASD and ADHD in Early Development
subsections.subsection_title: Distinctive features: social motivation vs. hyperactivity/impulsivity
subsections.content:
A core distinction between ASD and ADHD in early development lies in the nature of social motivation versus behavioral disinhibition. Infants later diagnosed with ASD often exhibit reduced social motivation, characterized by diminished eye contact, limited social smiling, and reduced initiation of joint attention—behaviors that reflect an intrinsic lack of interest in social reciprocity rather than an inability to regulate behavior ref [40]. In contrast, infants who later develop ADHD typically display age-appropriate social engagement but struggle with impulse control and motor hyperactivity, manifesting as excessive movement, difficulty remaining seated, and interruptive behaviors that emerge as regulatory demands increase ref [60]. These differences are evident even in the first year of life, with social attention deficits predicting later ASD diagnosis, while motor overactivity and poor inhibitory control are more strongly linked to ADHD outcomes ref [55].

Neurobiological evidence further supports this divergence: atypical activation in social brain networks, including the superior temporal sulcus and fusiform face area, is more consistently observed in infants at risk for ASD, whereas dysregulation in frontostriatal circuits governing inhibitory control is more prominent in those at risk for ADHD ref [52]. Longitudinal studies confirm that while both groups may show overlapping attentional difficulties, the underlying drivers differ—social disengagement in ASD versus behavioral disinhibition in ADHD ref [48]. This distinction has critical implications for early intervention, as therapies targeting social motivation (e.g., joint attention training) are less effective for children whose primary challenge is hyperactivity and impulsivity, which require behavioral regulation strategies ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Convergent and Divergent Pathways: Overlap and Distinction Between ASD and ADHD in Early Development
subsections.subsection_title: Developmental trajectories of comorbidity
subsections.content:
Longitudinal studies reveal that comorbidity between ASD and ADHD often emerges through divergent developmental pathways, with some children exhibiting early signs of both conditions, while others develop symptoms sequentially. Infants with dual familial risk for ASD and ADHD are more likely to show co-occurring attentional and social-communicative deficits by 12–18 months, predicting a dual diagnosis by age 3–4 ref [69]. However, a subset of children initially diagnosed with ASD later develop prominent hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, suggesting a trajectory of symptom expansion rather than convergence ref [23]. Conversely, children with early ADHD symptoms may acquire social communication difficulties over time, particularly if regulatory deficits impair peer interaction and learning opportunities ref [24].

Neurodevelopmental trajectories are further modulated by genetic and environmental factors; children with high polygenic risk scores for both disorders show earlier and more persistent co-occurring symptoms than those with risk for only one condition ref [48]. Brain connectivity studies indicate that children with persistent comorbidity exhibit atypical integration of fronto-striatal and default mode networks, distinct from those with ASD-only or ADHD-only profiles ref [2]. Early regulatory difficulties, including sleep and emotional dysregulation, are common in both trajectories and may serve as transdiagnostic markers ref [28].

Importantly, early intervention targeting executive function and emotional regulation may alter the trajectory of comorbidity, particularly when initiated before age 3 ref [23]. These findings challenge categorical diagnostic boundaries and support a dimensional model of neurodevelopmental risk, where comorbidity reflects overlapping vulnerabilities rather than distinct disorders.
